issues.legal_issue: The statutory finality of an administrative order does not displace a revision power provided in the same chapter.
material_facts: An Assistant Custodian determined on the merits that the property owner was a non-evacuee and owner of the property.
A later notice proposed revising that determination on grounds that it had been obtained through fraud and illegality.
The finality provision and the revision provision were both in Chapter V.
issues.conclusion: The earlier order was not immune from revision; the finality provision did not take away the revision power.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 27 and 28 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, orders are final subject to what is expressly provided in Chapter V. Because both provisions occur in Chapter V, Section 28 does not take away the revision power under Section 27. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.administrative_revision_of_custodian_ord: An authority began an administrative revision of an order made by a custodian.
predicates.finality_rule_subject_to_chapter_excepti: The governing finality rule makes orders final subject to exceptions provided in a specified chapter.
predicates.revision_power_in_same_chapter: The governing enactment places the power to revise the order in that same chapter.
predicates.revision_power_not_displaced_by_finality: The revision power remains available despite the finality rule.

issues.definition: When an administrative revision concerns a custodian order and the finality rule is subject to exceptions in the chapter that contains the revision power, the revision power remains available.

issues.legal_issue: The restriction on making new declarations of evacuee property does not bar revision proceedings concerning property for which proceedings were already pending at the relevant cutoff.
material_facts: An ex-parte declaration that the property owner was an evacuee and that the property was evacuee property was set aside on appeal.
Proceedings concerning the property were therefore pending at the statutory cutoff.
The Assistant Custodian later decided the matter on its merits, and a subsequent notice sought revision of that existing order rather than an initial declaration.
issues.conclusion: The statutory restriction did not bar the notice seeking revision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7A of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, barred declarations of evacuee property after the specified cutoff, but its proviso excluded property in respect of which proceedings were pending at that cutoff. Because the earlier ex-parte order had been set aside, proceedings concerning the property were pending then. The provision did not bar a later notice under Section 27 to revise the resulting order. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.revision_proceeding: An authority initiated a proceeding to revise an existing administrative determination about property.
predicates.property_proceedings_pending_at_cutoff: Proceedings concerning the property remained pending at the relevant statutory cutoff.
predicates.revision_notice_seeks_review_not_initial: The notice sought review of an existing determination rather than an initial declaration about the property.
predicates.cutoff_restriction_does_not_bar_revision: The cutoff restriction does not bar the revision notice.

issues.definition: When a revision proceeding concerns property whose proceedings were pending at the cutoff and the notice seeks review of an existing determination, the cutoff restriction does not bar the notice.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory revision power that is not limited by time is not barred merely because the revision notice was issued years after the challenged order.
material_facts: The order proposed to be revised was made in 1956.
The revision notice was issued several years later, in 1964.
The Court held that the applicable revision power was not curtailed by any limitation of time.
issues.conclusion: The revision proceeding was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, imposed no limitation of time on the revision power. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.statutory_revision_proceeding: An authority initiated a revision proceeding under a statutory power.
predicates.governing_enactment_sets_no_time_limit: The governing enactment sets no time limit for exercising the revision power.
predicates.revision_not_barred_by_lapse_of_time: The revision proceeding is not barred merely because time has passed.

issues.definition: When a statutory revision proceeding is governed by an enactment that sets no time limit, the proceeding is not barred merely because time has passed.

issues.legal_issue: A notice issued within the custodian administrative hierarchy to examine the legality or propriety of an order, including on an allegation of fraud, is within the authorities' jurisdiction and is not subject to quashing by certiorari absent excess or usurpation of jurisdiction.
material_facts: The Deputy Custodian General issued a notice proposing revision of an Assistant Custodian's order on allegations that the order had been obtained through fraud, forged documents, and perjured evidence.
The owner challenged the notice and the order rejecting her objections, including on the ground that the notice had not been issued by the Custodian General.

The statute placed custodians under the general superintendence and control of the Custodian General and authorized the relevant authorities to call for records to examine the legality or propriety of an order.
The alleged fraud was a factual matter, and the owner remained able to establish that she had properly obtained the order.
issues.conclusion: The notice was validly made within the authorities' jurisdiction, and certiorari would not lie; the owner could contest the factual allegation of fraud in the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(b), 2(c), 5, 6(2), and 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, define the relevant offices, provide for appointment, place custodians under the Custodian General's general superintendence and control, and confer revision authority. The relevant authorities may call for records to examine the legality or propriety of a custodian's order. Because the authorities had jurisdiction to issue the notice, and there was neither excess nor usurpation of jurisdiction, certiorari would not lie. Fraud was a question of fact that the affected person could contest. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

rule.if: certiorari_challenge_to_revision_notice and authority_empowered_to_review_custodian_orders and notice_investigates_alleged_fraud and not jurisdiction_exceeded_or_usurped

predicates.certiorari_challenge_to_revision_notice: A person sought certiorari to quash a notice initiating revision of an administrative order.
predicates.authority_empowered_to_review_custodian_: The relevant authority was empowered to examine the legality or propriety of a custodian's order.
predicates.notice_investigates_alleged_fraud: The notice sought to investigate an allegation that the order had been obtained by fraud.
predicates.jurisdiction_exceeded_or_usurped: The authority issuing the notice acted beyond or usurped its jurisdiction.
predicates.notice_within_jurisdiction_and_certiorar: The notice was within the authority's jurisdiction and is not quashed by certiorari.

issues.definition: When a certiorari challenge concerns a revision notice issued by an authority empowered to review custodian orders to investigate alleged fraud, and the authority did not exceed or usurp jurisdiction, the notice is within jurisdiction and certiorari is unavailable.
